From your roof to the edge

One flight out past the Moon, the planets and the stars, and one flight home.

Open the trip: From your roof to the edge

Your roof, tonight

This is the sky over your own place as tonight's dark arrives. Every point of light up there is somewhere. We are going to fly out past all of them, and after the first lift off the ground the camera will not cut once.

The Earth

Everyone you know is on this ball, 12 742 kilometres across. The satellites round it are where they are right now. From here on, keep your eye on the middle of the screen.

The Moon's orbit

The Moon goes round the Earth about 384 400 kilometres out, once in 27.3 days. Light crosses that gap in 1.3 seconds. Nobody has travelled further from home than this.

The planets

The Earth has shrunk to a dot on the third ring. Neptune, on the outer ring, is thirty times as far from the Sun as we are, and sunlight takes four hours to reach it.

The Oort cloud's distance

The planets are now inside one pixel. Comets come from a cloud of icy bodies thought to lie between 5 000 and 100 000 times the Earth's distance from the Sun. Nothing is drawn here because none of them has ever been seen in place.

The nearest stars

The Sun is one star among its neighbours. The nearest, Proxima Centauri, is 4.2 light-years away, and its two companions are the nearest stars you can see without a telescope. Each point here is a star at its measured distance.

How far our radio has got

The sphere marks how far radio from the Earth can have travelled since Marconi's signal crossed the Atlantic on 12 December 1901. It grows by one light-year a year. Out here the signal is far too faint to pick up. Everything humans have ever broadcast is inside it.

The Milky Way

Between one and four hundred billion stars, and the Sun is one of them, about 27 000 light-years from the centre. The shape is a model built from measurements. Nobody has seen our galaxy from outside.

The Local Group

Our galaxy and Andromeda, 2.5 million light-years apart, are the two large members of a group of more than a hundred galaxies, most of them small. Gravity holds this group together while the universe around it expands.

The oldest light

The sphere is the edge of what can be seen at all, about 46 billion light-years away now. No light has travelled for longer than 13.8 billion years: space stretched while it came. The microwave background, released about 380 000 years after the Big Bang, reaches us from just inside it. It is a horizon around us, not a wall. Every place has its own.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
